::: {.lead}
Every digital task in this course begins with two questions: *who am I to the
system?* and *where is my work stored?* This lab session answers both. It
explains how a university account identifies a student to many services at
once, how files are organised in folders and addressed by paths, how to read
file types and sizes, how to name and organise work so that it can be found
months later, and how cloud storage, synchronization and backup protect it.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary account authentication single-sign-on file folder file-path file-extension file-size cloud-storage synchronization backup >}}

## 2.1 Digital identity and the university account

An **account** is the record by which a service knows its user: an identifier
(the username, often an e-mail address), a means of proving identity, and the
data and permissions attached to it. Together, a person's accounts and the
information linked to them form their **digital identity**.

**Authentication** is the act of proving that one is the owner of an account.
Systems use three kinds of evidence, called *factors*: something you **know**
(a password or PIN), something you **have** (a phone that receives a code, a
security key) and something you **are** (a fingerprint or a face). Using two
different factors is called two-factor or **multi-factor authentication**
(MFA); week 3 studies it in detail.

A university offers many services: e-mail, the e-learning platform, cloud
storage, office applications, the library. Instead of one password per
service, most universities use **single sign-on (SSO)**: the student
authenticates once with the university account and is then trusted by all
connected services (@fig-sso).

![Single sign-on: one authentication with the university account gives access to several connected services.](images/sso.png){#fig-sso width=84%}

SSO is convenient and safer — one strong password is easier to protect than
ten weak ones — but it also concentrates risk: whoever steals the university
password reaches every service. This makes good habits on **shared lab
computers** essential:

- sign out of every service, and of the browser, at the end of the session;
- never let the browser remember the password on a shared computer;
- use a private (incognito) window when you must sign in on someone else's
  device;
- lock the screen when you leave the computer, even for a minute.

## 2.2 Files, folders and paths

A **file** is a named sequence of bytes kept in storage: a document, an image,
a program. A **folder** (or *directory*) groups files and other folders. Since
folders can contain folders, the storage of a computer forms a **tree**: one
top-level folder, the *root*, branches into folders, which branch again, down
to the files at the leaves (@fig-tree).

![A folder tree for course work. The highlighted path leads from the root to one file.](images/folder-tree.png){#fig-tree width=86%}

The **path** of a file is its address in this tree: the sequence of folders
from a starting point to the file, separated by a special character. Windows
separates folders with a backslash and starts from a drive letter; macOS,
Linux, Android and web addresses use a forward slash.

| System | Example path |
|---|---|
| Windows | `C:\Users\Sara\Documents\Courses\Digital-Skills\week-01\cv.docx` |
| macOS | `/Users/sara/Documents/Courses/Digital-Skills/week-01/cv.docx` |
| cloud (in the browser) | `My files > Courses > Digital-Skills > week-01 > cv.docx` |

: The same file addressed on different systems. {#tbl-paths}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Absolute and relative paths"}
An **absolute path** starts from the root and identifies a file uniquely, for
example `/Users/sara/Courses/Digital-Skills/week-01/cv.docx`. A **relative
path** starts from the current folder; from the folder `Digital-Skills`, the
same file is `week-01/cv.docx`. The name `..` means "the parent folder".
:::

### File types and extensions

The part of a file name after the last dot is the **file extension**. It tells
the operating system which program opens the file.

![Common file types and the units of file size.](images/file-types.png){#fig-types width=92%}

| Extension | Type | Typical program |
|---|---|---|
| `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.txt` | documents | Word, a PDF reader, a text editor |
| `.xlsx`, `.csv` | spreadsheets, tables | Excel, any spreadsheet |
| `.pptx` | presentations | PowerPoint |
| `.png`, `.jpg`, `.svg` | images | an image viewer or editor |
| `.mp3`, `.wav`, `.mp4` | audio, video | a media player |
| `.zip` | compressed archive | the file manager |
| `.exe`, `.apk` | programs, apps | the operating system — run only from trusted sources |

: Common file extensions. {#tbl-ext}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Trusting the icon instead of the extension. Windows hides known extensions by
default, so a malicious file named `invoice.pdf.exe` appears as `invoice.pdf`
with a document-like icon. Showing file extensions in the file manager is one
of the simplest security settings a student can make.
:::

### File sizes

Storage is measured in **bytes** (B); one byte is 8 bits. Larger units follow:
kilobyte (KB), megabyte (MB), gigabyte (GB), terabyte (TB). Two conventions
exist. Storage manufacturers use powers of 1000 (1 GB = 10^9^ bytes), while
operating systems traditionally count in powers of 1024 (1 GiB = 2^30^ bytes,
written GiB by standards bodies but often shown as "GB").

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Why a 128 GB phone shows less"}
1. The manufacturer's 128 GB is $128 \times 10^9$ bytes.
2. The phone counts in units of $2^{30} = 1\,073\,741\,824$ bytes.
3. $128 \times 10^9 / 1\,073\,741\,824 \approx 119.2$ — the phone reports about
   **119 GB**, before the operating system and preinstalled apps take their
   share. No storage is missing; only the unit differs.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — Will the files fit?"}
A student must upload a portfolio: 24 photos of 3.5 MB each, a 180 MB video
and a 2 MB CV. The e-learning platform accepts at most 250 MB per submission.

1. Photos: $24 \times 3.5 = 84$ MB.
2. Total: $84 + 180 + 2 = 266$ MB.
3. The submission is 16 MB too large. Compressing the photos to 2 MB each
   saves $24 \times 1.5 = 36$ MB, giving 230 MB, which fits.
:::

## 2.3 Naming and organising files

A file that cannot be found is as good as lost. Professionals follow a few
rules for **file names**:

1. **Be descriptive and consistent**: the name says what the file is, in the
   same pattern every time.
2. **Avoid spaces and special characters** (`/ \ : * ? " < > |`), which some
   systems forbid and web addresses mangle; use hyphens or underscores.
3. **Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD** (ISO 8601), so that alphabetical order is
   also chronological order.
4. **Number versions** (`v01`, `v02`) instead of `final`, `final2`,
   `final-really`.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — Improving file names"}
| Poor name | Better name |
|---|---|
| `New Document (3).docx` | `2026-10-21_DS_week01_cv_v01.docx` |
| `final final.pptx` | `2026-11-12_pitch-deck_v03.pptx` |
| `IMG_4821.jpg` | `2026-10-21_lab-desk-photo.jpg` |

Sorted alphabetically, the better names also appear in date order, and each
name tells its course, week, content and version.
:::

Folders deserve the same care. A good structure is shallow (rarely more than
four levels), mirrors the way the work is organised, and is the same for every
project. @fig-tree shows a structure for this diploma: one folder per course,
one per week, plus a folder for shared resources.

The same principles apply to professional work. A small game project, for
example, is usually organised by *kind of content* rather than by date:
`docs` for the design document and plans, `art` for images and models,
`audio` for music and sound effects, `builds` for the versions that are
tested, and `archive` for material that is no longer used but must be kept.
Everyone in the team then knows where to look, and a new member can find
their way on the first day.

## 2.4 Cloud storage, synchronization and backup

**Cloud storage** keeps files on servers of a provider — for a university
usually Microsoft OneDrive or Google Drive — reachable from any device after
signing in. Its main advantages are access from anywhere, easy sharing (week
2) and protection against the loss of a single device. Its limits are a
storage **quota**, the need for an Internet connection (unless files are
marked for offline use) and dependence on the provider's rules.

**Synchronization** keeps the same files identical on several devices and in
the cloud: a change made on the lab computer appears on the student's phone a
few seconds later. Synchronization is not the same as **backup**
(@fig-sync-backup).

![Synchronization copies every change everywhere — including mistakes. A backup is an independent copy that a mistake does not reach.](images/sync-backup.png){#fig-sync-backup width=90%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Synchronization and backup"}
**Synchronization** makes several copies identical: if a file is deleted or
damaged in one place, the deletion or damage is copied to all places. A
**backup** is an *independent* copy kept so that data can be restored after
loss, damage, deletion or attack.
:::

Many cloud services soften this difference with a *recycle bin* and a
*version history*, which keep deleted files and earlier versions for a limited
time. These features help, but they do not replace a real backup. A widely
used rule is the **3-2-1 rule**: keep **3** copies of important data, on **2**
different kinds of storage, with **1** copy in a different place.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.4 — A deleted project folder"}
A student keeps a game-design project in a synchronized cloud folder and
deletes it by mistake on the lab computer.

1. Synchronization deletes it on the laptop and the phone within seconds.
2. The cloud recycle bin still holds it for a limited period (often 30 days
   or more): it can be restored — if the student notices in time.
3. Had the student also followed the 3-2-1 rule — for example a weekly copy on
   a USB drive kept at home — the project would be safe even after the bin was
   emptied.
:::

## Lab session: setting up your digital workspace

In the lab, each student signs in with the university account, opens the
university's cloud storage, creates the folder structure of @fig-tree, and
uploads, renames and restores a test file. The interactive lesson lists the
steps; the mini-game *Path Finder* practises paths.

Evans, Martin and Poatsy, *Technology in Action*, 18th ed., chapters on using
the Internet and cloud services, and on file management in operating systems.

## Exercises

1. Name the three kinds of authentication factor and give one example of
   each.
2. Explain single sign-on, one advantage and one risk.
3. List four safe habits for shared lab computers.
4. Write the absolute path of `notes.docx` in the folder `week-02` of
   `Digital-Skills`, inside `Courses`, inside `Documents` of user `ali`, on
   macOS.
5. From the folder `Courses/Digital-Skills`, write the relative path to
   `Courses/Game-Math/week-01/hw1.pdf`.
6. Which program opens each file: `budget.xlsx`, `trailer.mp4`,
   `levels.zip`, `logo.svg`?
7. Why is `photo.jpg.exe` dangerous, and which setting helps to detect it?
8. A memory card is sold as 256 GB. About how many GB does a computer that
   counts in powers of 1024 report?
9. Rename `My Project FINAL (2).pptx`, created on 3 November 2026 for the
   Digital Skills pitch, using the rules of §2.3.
10. Explain why synchronization is not a backup, and state the 3-2-1 rule.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Know (password), have (phone with a code), are (fingerprint).
2. One authentication gives access to all connected services; advantage: one strong password; risk: a stolen password opens everything.
3. Sign out; do not save passwords; use a private window; lock the screen.
4. `/Users/ali/Documents/Courses/Digital-Skills/week-02/notes.docx`.
5. `../Game-Math/week-01/hw1.pdf`.
6. A spreadsheet (Excel); a media player; the file manager (archive); an image viewer or a browser.
7. It is a program disguised as an image; show file extensions.
8. $256 \times 10^9 / 2^{30} \approx 238$ GB.
9. For example `2026-11-03_DS_pitch-deck_v01.pptx`.
10. Synchronization copies deletions and damage to every copy; a backup is independent. 3 copies, 2 kinds of storage, 1 off-site.
:::
